questions.q: Pressing RETURN at an empty GDB prompt runs the most recent previous command again.
questions.explain: RETURN repeats the last command. This is handy when you are moving through code with a series of next or step commands.

questions.q: You have typed a unique prefix of a GDB command. Which key asks GDB to complete the command line?
questions.explain: GDB supports command-line completion with the TAB key.

questions.q: What short abbreviation can you type instead of the full command `print x`? Give the whole command.
questions.explain: `p` is the short form of `print`. In the same way, `l` stands for `list` and `n` for `next`.

questions.q: What do the up and down arrow keys do at the GDB prompt?
choices: Scroll through previous GDB command lines
Step forward or backward one source line
Scroll the source listing up or down
questions.explain: The arrow keys scroll through earlier command lines, so you don't have to type them again.

questions.q: Which command shows GDB's help information about breakpoints?
questions.explain: `help <topic or command>` shows help for that topic or command. `info break` lists the breakpoints you have set; it does not show help.

questions.q: The program is paused on a line that calls a function. What is the difference between `step` and `next` here?
choices: `step` treats the call as a single line; `next` enters the function
`step` enters the called function; `next` runs the whole call and pauses at the following line
Both enter the function, but `next` skips its first line
Neither enters the function; `step` just prints more information
questions.explain: `step` steps into the called function. `next` treats the call as one line and pauses once the call has returned.

questions.q: After `step 10`, the program may end up paused inside a function that was called from the original pause point.
questions.explain: With `step <count>`, lines run inside a called function count toward the total, so execution can stop inside that function.

questions.q: How do you start the debugged program from the beginning with the command-line arguments 2, 40, and 100?
questions.explain: `run <command line arguments>` starts the program from the beginning and passes it those arguments.

questions.q: The program is paused in main.c. You want a breakpoint at line 34 of gofish.c, another source file of the same program. Which command does this?
questions.explain: `break <filename>:<line>` sets a breakpoint in a particular file. A bare `break 34` refers to line 34 of the current file.

questions.q: Write the command that runs the program until it reaches source line 50.
questions.explain: `until <line>` keeps executing until execution reaches that line number.

questions.q: The program is paused at a breakpoint. Which commands resume execution from that point?
questions.explain: `continue` (short form `cont`) resumes from the breakpoint. `run` restarts the program from the beginning, and `quit` exits GDB.

questions.q: What does `next 3` do?
choices: Executes the next 3 lines, treating any function call as a single line
Executes the next 3 lines, stepping into any function calls
Continues to line 3 of the program
questions.explain: `next <count>` works like `step <count>`, except that each function call counts as one line and GDB doesn't enter it.

questions.q: Which commands show the contents of the call stack, meaning the sequence of function calls at the current point of execution?
questions.explain: `where`, `backtrace`, and `bt` are three names for the same command. `frame` changes the current stack frame, and `list` shows source code.

questions.q: When the program pauses, which stack frame's context is GDB in by default?
choices: Frame 0, the frame at the top of the stack
The frame at the bottom of the stack
Frame 1, the caller of the current function
questions.explain: By default the program pauses in frame 0, which is the frame at the top of the stack.

questions.q: Why would you usually run a command like `frame 3`?
choices: To set a breakpoint 3 frames up the stack
To print the parameters and local variables of a different function on the stack
To delete the top 3 stack frames
To run the program until it has made 3 more function calls
questions.explain: `frame <num>` moves into another stack frame's context. Users typically do this so they can print that function's parameters and local variables.

questions.q: Write the command that lists source code lines 30 through 100.
questions.explain: `list <start> <end>` lists that range of line numbers.

questions.q: What does `list main` display?
choices: The lines around the beginning of the function main
The stack frames belonging to main
questions.explain: `list <func-name>` shows the lines around the beginning of that function.

questions.q: What is the difference between `delete` and `clear`?
choices: `delete` removes a breakpoint by its number; `clear` removes the breakpoint at a source location such as a line or function
`delete` removes a breakpoint permanently; `clear` only disables it
`delete` takes a line number; `clear` takes a breakpoint number
There is none; they are aliases
questions.explain: `delete <bpnum>` uses the breakpoint's number. `clear <line>` and `clear <func-name>` use a location in the source code.

questions.q: What does `ignore 2 5` do?
choices: Ignores breakpoint 5 the next 2 times it is hit
Doesn't pause at breakpoint 2 the next 5 times it is hit
Ignores line 2 for the next 5 iterations of a loop
questions.explain: The syntax is `ignore <bpnum> <num>`. GDB skips breakpoint <bpnum> for its next <num> hits.

questions.q: Running `delete` with no arguments deletes all breakpoints.
questions.explain: `delete <bpnum>` removes one breakpoint. A bare `delete` removes all of them.

questions.q: After `disable 3`, you can turn breakpoint 3 back on with `enable 3`.
questions.explain: Disabling a breakpoint doesn't delete it, so `enable <bnums>` can turn it back on.

questions.q: Commands like `disable`, `ignore`, `condition`, and `delete` need breakpoint numbers. Which command lists the breakpoints with their numbers?
questions.explain: `info break` (or `info breakpoints`) lists every breakpoint with its number, type, enabled status, address, and location.

questions.q: Breakpoint 1 is inside a loop. Write the command that makes it pause only when the expression i > 1000 is true.
questions.explain: `condition <bpnum> <exp>` makes breakpoint <bpnum> transfer control to GDB only when <exp> is true.

questions.q: Which of these are good uses for a conditional breakpoint?
choices: Pausing inside a loop only after a certain number of iterations
Pausing only when a variable holds a value that matters for debugging
Permanently removing a breakpoint from a line
Showing the values in the hardware registers
questions.explain: A condition on a loop counter or on a variable's value stops the program only at the moments you care about.

questions.q: What does `print/d 0x1c` print?
questions.explain: Hex 1c is 16 + 12 = 28, and /d prints it as a signed decimal integer.

questions.q: What does `print/x 123` print?
questions.explain: 123 = 7*16 + 11, so in hex it is 0x7b. 1111011 is what `print/t 123` would print.

questions.q: What does `print 0x12 + 2` print? (No format letter is given, so the result is shown in decimal.)
questions.explain: Hex 12 is 18 in decimal, and 18 + 2 = 20.

questions.q: What does `print 0b101 + 3` print?
questions.explain: The 0b prefix marks a binary literal. 0b101 is 5, and 5 + 3 = 8.

questions.q: What does `print/c 99` print?
questions.explain: /c prints the value as an ASCII character, and ASCII 99 is 'c'. Going the other way, `print (int)'c'` prints 99.

questions.q: Which format letter makes `print` show a value in binary? (For example, it prints 123 as 1111011.)
questions.explain: `print/t <exp>` prints in binary. /x is hexadecimal, /d is signed decimal, and /c is a character.

questions.q: Why does `print *(int *)0x8ff4bc10` include the `(int *)` cast?
choices: Without a type, GDB doesn't know how to dereference the address
GDB only accepts addresses written in decimal
The cast makes GDB print the result in hexadecimal
The cast is optional and only for readability
questions.explain: A bare address has no type. Casting it to `int *` tells GDB to read an int at that location.

questions.q: If `ptr` is declared as `int *`, you have to write `print *(int *)ptr` to see the int it points to; `print *ptr` won't work.
questions.explain: GDB knows the declared type of the pointer variable, so `print *ptr` works and needs no cast.

questions.q: Which command prints the value stored in the eax hardware register?
questions.explain: In GDB expressions, register names start with a $.

questions.q: `print` can evaluate any C expression, even one that does not appear anywhere in the program's code.
questions.explain: `print` isn't limited to program variables. For example, `p i+3` prints the value of i plus 3.

questions.q: How does the `x` command differ from `print`?
choices: `x` treats its argument as an address and shows the value stored at that address
`x` evaluates expressions, while `print` only shows variables
`x` changes the value stored in memory
questions.explain: `x` reads its argument as an address and dereferences it. That is why `x &temp` shows the same value as `print temp`.

questions.q: You run `x/c ptr`, and later run `x ptr2` with no format given. Which format does the second command use?
choices: The /c format, because x's formatting is sticky
None; x requires a format each time
questions.explain: x's formatting is sticky. GDB remembers the last format and applies it to later x commands that don't specify one.

questions.q: In `x/nfu`, which unit letters are paired with the correct size?
questions.explain: The units are b = byte, h = 2 bytes (halfword), w = 4 bytes (word), and g = 8 bytes (giant).

questions.q: What does `x/10dh 0x1234` display?
choices: 10 short (2-byte) values starting at address 0x1234, in decimal
The value of variable h, 10 times
questions.explain: Here n = 10 is the repeat count, f = d is decimal, and u = h is 2-byte units.

questions.q: `s1 = "Hello There"` is stored at address 0x40062d. What does `x/4c s1` show?
questions.explain: /4c examines 4 characters, and each one is shown with its ASCII value and the character itself.

questions.q: Right after `x/s s1`, you want to look at the same memory as a 4-byte int. Why do you need `x/wd s1` and not just `x/d s1`?
choices: x/s set the unit size to bytes, and because formatting is sticky the w has to be given explicitly
The d format is not allowed without a unit letter
s1 is a string, so x can't read it as an int
The order of the letters matters, so w has to come first
questions.explain: x/s leaves the unit size set to bytes. Since the setting is sticky, you need w to switch back to 4-byte words.

questions.q: `s1 = "Hello There"`. The command `x/8d s1` prints the ASCII values of the first 8 characters. What is the 6th value printed?
questions.explain: The first 8 characters are H e l l o (space) T h, which print as 72 101 108 108 111 32 84 104. The 6th one is the space, ASCII 32.

questions.q: Which display-format letter makes `x` show memory as a string?
questions.explain: Some x display formats are s (string), i (instruction), x (hex), d (decimal), t (binary), and a (address).

questions.q: How does `display i` differ from `print i`?
choices: `display i` shows i automatically every time a breakpoint is reached
`display i` shows i only once, in hexadecimal
`display i` shows the type of i
`display i` shows i in a separate window
questions.explain: `display <exp>` shows the expression each time a breakpoint is reached. It uses the same expression syntax as print.

questions.q: x is an int. What does `whatis (x + 3.4)` report?
questions.explain: `whatis` shows an expression's type. Adding the double literal 3.4 to x gives a result of type double.

questions.q: Write the GDB command that changes the program variable x to the value of 123 * y.
questions.explain: The form is `set <variable> = <exp>`.

questions.q: Which of these can the `set` command assign a value to?
choices: A line of the source code
questions.explain: `set` can change a program variable, the value at a memory address, or a register. It cannot edit source code.

questions.q: Which command shows the argument variables of the current stack frame?
questions.explain: `info args` shows the arguments. `info locals` shows local variables, `info frame` shows details about the frame, and `info registers` shows register values.

questions.q: Write the `info` command that shows the values in the registers.
questions.explain: `info registers` shows register values. Run `help info` to see every info option.
